University of California, Berkeley

Golden Handcuffs make safer AI agents

Aram Ebtekar Email: aramebtech@gmail.com    Michael K. Cohen Email: mkcohen@berkeley.edu Affiliation: 
Abstract

Reinforcement learners can attain high reward through novel unintended strategies. We study a Bayesian mitigation for general environments: we expand the agent’s subjective reward range to include a large negative value −L-L, while the true environment’s rewards lie in [0,1][0,1]. After observing consistently high rewards, the Bayesian policy becomes risk-averse to novel schemes that plausibly lead to −L-L. We design a simple override mechanism that yields control to a safe mentor whenever the predicted value drops below a fixed threshold. We prove two properties of the resulting agent: (i) Capability: using mentor-guided exploration with vanishing frequency, the agent attains sublinear regret against its best mentor. (ii) Safety: no decidable low-complexity predicate is triggered by the optimizing policy before it is triggered by a mentor.

keywords
Safety, pessimism, reinforcement learning, Knightian uncertainty, Kolmogorov complexity, stopping complexity, Solomonoff induction, AIXI, explore-exploit dilemma, reward hacking

1 Introduction

AI agents are increasingly deployed in general environments, where the traditional Markov, ergodicity, and full-observability assumptions do not apply (Aslanides et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2026). In these settings, AIXI is the Bayesian policy that maximizes expected value under a universal prior based on Solomonoff (1964). Variants of AIXI can learn their environment with strong sample efficiency guarantees (Hutter, 2005; Hutter et al., 2024; Meulemans et al., 2025). While AIXI is incomputable, it has inspired computable approximations (Veness et al., 2011). It can be viewed as an idealization of the simplicity bias exhibited by large neural networks (Buzaglo et al., 2024; Lotfi et al., 2024; Mingard et al., 2025), making AIXI suitable for mathematical modeling of advanced AI agents.

A fundamental problem with general environments is that, in order to asymptotically learn an optimal policy, an agent must eventually explore every finite sequence of actions, even if some lead to irrecoverable states (Cohen et al., 2021).11 1 Unlike its asymptotically optimal variants (Lattimore and Hutter, 2011; Cohen et al., 2019), AIXI’s exploration is prior-directed and may cease prematurely; whether it avoids traps or is steered into them depends on its prior (Orseau, 2010; Leike and Hutter, 2015). Once we have a near-optimal policy, a second problem emerges: the policy optimizes a value function that is not fully aligned with the designer’s intended objective, since the latter resists precise specification. It has been argued that a sufficiently capable reward maximizer can be expected to “wirehead” its reward channel, “reward hack” in unanticipated and harmful ways, or seek power to influence future outcomes (Orseau and Ring, 2011; Hadfield-Menell et al., 2017; Zhuang and Hadfield-Menell, 2020; Turner et al., 2021; Everitt et al., 2021; Cohen et al., 2022a; Russell, 2022).

We address both problems with a pessimistic variant of AIXI that occasionally defers to one or more safe mentor policies. Whereas optimistic algorithms that encourage exploration (Sunehag and Hutter, 2015) are vulnerable to traps and misspecification, our pessimistic agent does not initiate exploration on its own. By deferring exploratory actions to mentors, the agent avoids irrecoverable states that the mentors avoid, and cannot act on misspecification in regimes that the mentors would not enter.

To be more precise, we scale AIXI’s observed rewards upward, so that they concentrate near the top of the range the prior considers possible. We think of our agent as being bound by “Golden Handcuffs”: after learning from experience to expect high rewards, the agent becomes averse to exploring novel situations in which the possibility of low rewards cannot be ruled out. We formalize novelty in terms of the stopping complexity, first introduced by Vovk and Pavlovic (2017) and Andreev et al. (2018). Intuitively, the novelty of a moment in time is given by how short we can make a computable criterion that, while scanning the agent-environment interaction history, halts at that particular moment. Such a criterion distinguishes the present moment from the past; at these novel moments, the future under the universal prior becomes ambiguous, so our agent is pessimistic about what follows.

The Golden Handcuffs agent follows a policy πGH{\pi^{\mathrm{GH}}} that usually matches this pessimistic AIXI. It defers to a mentor policy occasionally, at random times for exploration, as well as anytime that it loses confidence in achieving rewards near the top of the range. This enables us to prove that the agent learns to perform at least as well as the best mentor, with sublinear regret of order T23+ϵT^{\frac{2}{3}+\epsilon} by time TT (\Crefthm:capability), and never takes unsafe simple actions that the mentors would never take (\Crefcor:safety).

The paper is organized as follows. In \Crefsec:related, we review additional related works. In \Crefsec:prelim, we introduce notation. In \Crefsec:agent, we present the new Golden Handcuffs agent, which interleaves Bayesian expected reward maximization with mentor actions. In \Crefsec:capability, we prove that despite using the mentor policies with vanishing frequency, the agent achieves low regret against an adaptive selection of the best mentor policy. In \Crefsec:safety, we prove that simple unprecedented events can only be triggered by a mentor, not by the optimizing policy. If the mentors are safe, this makes πGH{\pi^{\mathrm{GH}}} safe in the sense of avoiding actions that the mentors would avoid. In \Crefsec:discussion, we discuss the approach and its limitations, before concluding in \Crefsec:conclusion. Details of the capability proofs are relegated to \Crefapx:proofs.

2 Related work

Garcıa and Fernández (2015) and Russell (2022) survey different aspects of safety for RL agents, the former focusing on robustness in dangerous environments, and the latter on alignment with humans. Our Golden Handcuffs algorithm handles both cases by assigning negative value to novelty, which is a cue to both kinds of danger.

Some recent work combines optimism toward opportunities with pessimism against danger. To distinguish opportunities from danger in unknown environments, additional modeling assumptions are required (Curi et al., 2021; Bura et al., 2022; Wendl et al., ).

In fully general environments, an agent cannot guarantee safety on its own, so some form of external guidance is needed. Saunders et al. (2018) present Human Intervention RL (HIRL), initially allowing a human overseer to block catastropic actions, until an AI overseer trained on the human interventions is able to take over. Actions flagged by the overseer are assigned a negative reward. In contrast, our approach assigns negative rewards based on intrinsic novelty, and only requires the mentor(s) to know a safe action, not necessarily to recognize every catastrophic action.

Methods for learning to defer to human experts (Madras et al., 2018; Hemmer et al., 2023; Strong et al., 2025) were recently extended to the sequential setting (Joshi et al., 2023; Rayan and Tewari, 2025). These algorithms decide when to defer by comparing learned success rates of the AI model and human expert. In contrast, our notion of novelty captures what is sometimes called Knightian uncertainty, or epistemic ignorance about regimes for which the agent has no learned model (Knight, 1921). The universal prior lets us act under such ignorance within a fully Bayesian framework, in contrast to approaches based on max-min expected utility across multiple priors (Epstein and Wang, 2004; Hansen and Sargent, 2011; Kishishita et al., 2026).

Cohen et al. (2022b) study a regularized form of imitation learning that refuses to act when it has Knightian uncertainty about how the human would act. Coste et al. () maximize the worst-case among multiple reward models. Cohen et al. (2025) regularize RL, maximizing rewards subject to staying close to a demonstrated human policy, thus avoiding any action that the human would never take. In contrast to these works, our Golden Handcuffs agent straightforwardly maximizes expected value at almost all times, with the mentor(s) only intervening with vanishing frequency.

Our work is most closely related to Cohen and Hutter (2020). Recognizing the difficulty of formalizing alignment, they propose to contain the most severe risks within a definition of novelty related to stopping complexity, albeit without mentioning the latter. Their agent is more complicated than ours, both in choosing when to query the mentor (based on Thompson sampling), and in instilling pessimism (by pessimizing over world models instead of simply scaling the reward channel). They only prove their agent’s performance to be asymptotically competitive with one mentor, without convergence rates like ours. Their safety bound is also looser, adding a dependence on the environment’s complexity.

4 Agent definition

Our Bayesian reinforcement learning agent models its environment as a mixture ξ\xi over countably many models ν\nu, with weights wν>0w_{\nu}>0 satisfying ∑νwν≤1\sum_{\nu}w_{\nu}\leq 1:

ξ(or<t∥a<t)=∑νwνν(or<t∥a<t),\xi(o\;\!\!r_{<t}\parallel a_{<t})=\sum_{\nu}w_{\nu}\nu(o\;\!\!r_{<t}\parallel a_{<t}), (3)

The true environment μ\mu is assumed to be included in the mixture, with weight wμw_{\mu}.

Fix a discount factor γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1). For a policy π\pi and environment ν\nu, the value function is the expected normalized discounted sum of future rewards:

Vνπ​(h<t):=𝔼νπ​[(1−γ)​∑s=0∞γs​rt+s|h<t]V_{\nu}^{\pi}(h_{<t}):=\mathbb{E}_{\nu}^{\pi}\left[(1-\gamma)\sum_{s=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{s}r_{t+s}\,\Big|\,h_{<t}\right] (4)

Given the mixture prior ξ\xi, the Bayes ξ\xi-optimal policy is given by

πξ∗∈arg⁡maxπ​Vξπ​(h<t),\pi_{\xi}^{*}\in\arg\max_{\pi}V_{\xi}^{\pi}(h_{<t}),

with ties broken arbitrarily. Its expected total discounted reward is given by

Vξ∗​(h<t):=maxπ⁡Vξπ​(h<t).V_{\xi}^{*}(h_{<t}):=\max_{\pi}V_{\xi}^{\pi}(h_{<t}).

Note that this policy is optimal with respect to ξ\xi rather than the true unknown environment μ\mu. In fact, Leike and Hutter (2015) show that πξ∗\pi_{\xi}^{*} might never become μ\mu-optimal, even asymptotically, if it believes the cost of exploring is too high. Policies that explore more can become asymptotically optimal, but Cohen et al. (2021) show that such policies must eventually try every possible sequence of actions, even those that destroy the agent. Moreover, a truly μ\mu-optimal policy might be catastrophically misaligned: a strict reward maximizer would behave like a literalist genie, maximizing a formally specified value function at the expense of our intended objective (Hadfield-Menell et al., 2017; Turner et al., 2021; Zhuang and Hadfield-Menell, 2020; Everitt et al., 2021; Cohen et al., 2022a).

Instead, we propose selective exploration guided by a set of one or more trusted mentor policies 𝒯\mathcal{T}, so that the agent can learn to perform well without doing anything that would be unanimously avoided by the mentor policies. The mentors can be human operators that are available to take the wheel as needed, or trusted AI policies.

To complete the agent’s construction, let us review our two core desiderata. First, we want it to perform well despite not knowing μ\mu. By default, it will follow a reward-maximizing policy πξ∗\pi_{\xi}^{*} for some Bayesian prior ξ\xi; however, greedily exploiting ξ\xi risks neglecting some good strategies known by the mentor policies. To ensure sufficient safe exploration, at random intervals of decreasing frequency, the agent switches to following a rollout from one of the mentor policies.

Our second desideratum, for safety, is that the agent should avoid doing anything unprecedented. This is achieved by concentrating the values of reward percepts in the true environment μ\mu to the top of the range of subjectively possible rewards in ξ\xi. For example, if ξ\xi offers rewards from ℛ⊂[0, 1]\mathcal{R}\subset[0,\,1], we scale the true rewards to [1−δ, 1][1-\delta,\,1] for a small δ>0\delta>0. For ease of interpretability, we prefer instead to fix the true reward range to [0, 1][0,\,1], and get the same effect by letting the subjective mixture ξ\xi offer rewards from an expanded set ℛ⊂[−L, 1]\mathcal{R}\subset[-L,\,1] that includes a minimum element −L:=1−1/δ-L:=1-1/\delta. Either way, our agent is effectively bound by “Golden Handcuffs”, happy to continue receiving near-maximal rewards, and averse to any change that risks a massive loss, since there is little left to gain.

Whenever the ξ\xi-optimal policy’s value function is reasonably high (say above −1-1), it can be fairly confident that it will stay within the well-understood regime in which the likelihood of receiving −L-L reward has become small. If the value function gets too low, we can no longer be confident in the safety of πξ∗\pi_{\xi}^{*}, so we program the agent to follow a mentor policy until confidence is restored.

We denote the Golden Handcuffs agent’s policy by πGH{\pi^{\mathrm{GH}}}; \Crefalg:safe implements it in pseudocode. At each time step tt, πGH{\pi^{\mathrm{GH}}} chooses an action according to either the optimizing policy πξ∗\pi_{\xi}^{*} or one of the mentor policies τ∈𝒯\tau\in\mathcal{T}. Two conditions can trigger a mentor policy: (1) the safety trigger Vξ∗​(h<t)≤−1V^{*}_{\xi}(h_{<t})\leq-1, at which point we yield to any mentor for this step; and (2) the random trigger with probability η⁡(t)\eta(t), at which point we sample a random mentor τ∈𝒯\tau\in\mathcal{T} for the next H⁡(t)H(t) steps. Each mentor τ\tau has a preset probability wτw_{\tau} of being chosen, with ∑τ∈𝒯wτ=1\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}}w_{\tau}=1. According to a preset schedule, η\eta decreases and HH increases.

While we focus our analysis on \Crefalg:safe for its intuitive clarity, we expect minor variants of the Golden Handcuffs agent to behave similarly. For example, we can replace the negative rewards in ℛ\mathcal{R} with a single “hell” value, which overrides all future rewards and sets them to −L-L forever. We can also replace the trigger Vξ∗​(h<t)≤−1V^{*}_{\xi}(h_{<t})\leq-1 with a check that “hell” has a substantial likelihood of arising in the near future.

In \Crefeq:value, there are multiple ways to define the expected value of rtr_{t} when it is distributed according to a semimeasure: we can condition on rtr_{t} being defined, effectively normalizing the semimeasure; or we can treat rtr_{t} as having some default value whenever it is undefined. We use the default value 00 for simplicity, but expect our results to hold for the normalization as well as any default value in [−L, 1][-L,\,1]. Alternatively, we can confine the modeled rewards to [0, 1][0,\,1], but replace undefined rewards with a default of −L-L, equivalent to the “hell” state. This pessimistic expected value is an instance of the Choquet integral; see Wyeth and Hutter (2025).

5 Capability analysis

In order to analyze the policy πGH{\pi^{\mathrm{GH}}} from \Crefalg:safe, we need some additional notation. The behavior of this policy at time step tt depends not only on the history h<th_{<t}, but also on its internal state σt∈{0}∪(ℤ+×𝒯)\sigma_{t}\in\{0\}\cup(\mathbb{Z}^{+}\times\mathcal{T}). We write σt=0\sigma_{t}=0 if at the start of iteration tt the agent is not exploring, i.e., rollout_steps=0\texttt{rollout\_steps}=0. Otherwise, we write σt=(n,τ)\sigma_{t}=(n,\tau) to mean that the actions at:t+n−1a_{t:t+n-1} will be sampled from the mentor policy τ\tau. Note that we always have σ1=0\sigma_{1}=0. We write VνπGH​(h<t,σt)V_{\nu}^{\pi^{\mathrm{GH}}}(h_{<t},\sigma_{t}) for the expected value of policy πGH{\pi^{\mathrm{GH}}} in state σt\sigma_{t}, in an environment ν\nu starting from history h<th_{<t}. Marginalizing out the state variable recovers

VνπGH​(h<t):=𝔼νπGH​[VνπGH​(h<t,σt)∣h<t].V_{\nu}^{\pi^{\mathrm{GH}}}(h_{<t}):=\mathbb{E}_{\nu}^{\pi^{\mathrm{GH}}}\left[V_{\nu}^{\pi^{\mathrm{GH}}}(h_{<t},\sigma_{t})\mid h_{<t}\right]. (5)

Our main capability theorem says that, despite not knowing the true environment μ\mu, πGH{\pi^{\mathrm{GH}}} learns to become competitive with all of the mentor policies τ∈𝒯\tau\in\mathcal{T}. That is, at almost all time steps tt, VμπGH​(h<t)V_{\mu}^{\pi^{\mathrm{GH}}}(h_{<t}) approximates or exceeds maxτ∈𝒯ϵ⁡Vμτ​(h<t)\max_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}_{\epsilon}}V_{\mu}^{\tau}(h_{<t}), where the maximum is taken over all mentors with sufficient sampling weight 𝒯ϵ:={τ∈𝒯:wτ≥ϵ}\mathcal{T}_{\epsilon}:=\{\tau\in\mathcal{T}:\,w_{\tau}\geq\epsilon\}.

Since we cannot rule out the possibility that following τ\tau for a long time will lead to high rewards thereafter, such a guarantee requires exploration rollouts of length comparable to the effective discount time horizon of the agent. By increasing the horizon length H⁡(t)H(t) over time, we ensure that the approximation error vanishes asymptotically.

eq:weakoptimality says that starting from any of all but T23+ϵT^{\frac{2}{3}+\epsilon} of the first TT time steps tt, πGH{\pi^{\mathrm{GH}}} is competitive with the best non-negligibly weighted mentor policy. As a result, every mentor policy is eventually matched or outdone almost all of the time.

We defer the proof of \Crefthm:capability to \Crefapx:proofs. Here we outline some key results it uses. Since πGH{\pi^{\mathrm{GH}}} makes the optimizing policy yield to a mentor policy whenever Vξ∗​(h<t)≤−1V^{*}_{\xi}(h_{<t})\leq-1, we want to bound how often this occurs. Since the observed rewards are all non-negative, the Bayesian learner should become increasingly confident that future rewards will continue to be non-negative. Unfortunately, Cohen and Hutter (2020) explain that in the case of a Solomonoff prior, it is possible for one’s confidence in a long-horizon statement such as “all future rewards will be non-negative” to converge incredibly slowly, indeed more slowly than any computable function.

Fortunately, one’s confidence in a short-horizon statement such as “all near-future rewards will be non-negative” will typically become high much earlier on. Let

αt,u:=ℙξπ(ru≱0∣h1:t),\alpha_{t,u}:=\mathbb{P}_{\xi}^{\pi}(r_{u}\ngeq 0\mid h_{1:t}), (8)

where ru≱0r_{u}\ngeq 0 denotes the event that either ru<0r_{u}<0 or rur_{u} has no value at all, due to the environment model ceasing to emit percepts by time step uu.

Lemma 2.

Let π\pi be any policy and suppose Pμπ(∀t∈ℤ+,rt≥0)=1P_{\mu}^{\pi}(\forall t\in\mathbb{Z}^{+},\,r_{t}\geq 0)=1. Then for all s≥0s\geq 0,

𝔼μπ​[∑t=0∞αt,t+s]≤s​ln⁡1wμ.\mathbb{E}_{\mu}^{\pi}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\alpha_{t,\,t+s}\right]\leq s\ln\frac{1}{w_{\mu}}.

While we will not need this generalization, the event ru≱0r_{u}\not\geq 0 can in fact be replaced by any event that never occurs in the true environment μ\mu. In \Crefapx:proofs, we prove \Creflem:alpha, and then use it to show the following bound on the expected sum of ξ\xi-subjective probabilities that the safety trigger will hold a fixed number ss steps in the future. In particular, the case s=0s=0 bounds the expected number of times that Vξ∗​(h<t)≤−1V^{*}_{\xi}(h_{<t})\leq-1 holds.

Theorem 3.

Let π\pi be any policy and suppose Pμπ(∀t∈ℤ+,rt≥0)=1P_{\mu}^{\pi}(\forall t\in\mathbb{Z}^{+},\,r_{t}\geq 0)=1. Then for all s≥0s\geq 0,

𝔼μπ​[∑t=1∞ℙξπ​[Vξπ​(h<t+s)≤−1∣h<t]]≤L⁡(s+11−γ)​ln⁡1wμ.\mathbb{E}_{\mu}^{\pi}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\mathbb{P}_{\xi}^{\pi}\left[V_{\xi}^{\pi}(h_{<t+s})\leq-1\mid h_{<t}\right]\right]\leq L\left(s+\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\right)\ln\frac{1}{w_{\mu}}.

In particular (by setting s=0s=0),

𝔼μπ[#t:Vξ∗(h<t)≤−1]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mu}^{\pi}\left[\#t:\;V_{\xi}^{*}(h_{<t})\leq-1\right] ≤𝔼μπ[#t:Vξπ(h<t)≤−1]\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}_{\mu}^{\pi}\left[\#t:\;V_{\xi}^{\pi}(h_{<t})\leq-1\right]
=𝔼μπ​[∑t=1∞𝟙​(Vξπ​(h<t)≤−1)]≤L1−γ​ln⁡1wμ.\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mu}^{\pi}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\mathds{1}\left(V_{\xi}^{\pi}(h_{<t})\leq-1\right)\right]\leq\frac{L}{1-\gamma}\ln\frac{1}{w_{\mu}}.

On expectation, when \Crefalg:safe is run with the parameters in \labelcrefeq:exploreparams, only O⁡(T2/3​log⁡T)O(T^{2/3}\log T) of the first TT time steps are spent on exploratory mentor rollouts. And by \Crefthm:trigger, only a constant number of time steps defer to a mentor for safety. Thus, πGH{\pi^{\mathrm{GH}}} defers to mentors with asymptotically vanishing frequency, acting according to the reward-maximizing policy πξ∗\pi_{\xi}^{*} at all other times.

6 Safety analysis

Novel situations present the highest risk of misgeneralization. If the optimizing policy acts in a novel situation, it may optimize rewards for the wrong world model, risking harm to itself; or it may optimize rewards for a setting in which the reward signal is no longer aligned with our intent, thus acting against our values.

Recall that \Crefthm:capability depends on the weight wμw_{\mu} that the Bayesian prior assigns to the true environment μ\mu. An open-minded prior that considers all conceivable environments can perform relatively well on all of them. This open-mindedness is also key to safety, as it means that for any event EE which has not yet occurred, the agent cannot rule out the possibility that EE will trigger the minimal reward −L-L from then onward. This possibility drags down the value of any history in which EE has just occurred. Provided that LL is sufficiently large, this activates the safety trigger Vξ∗​(h<t)≤−1V_{\xi}^{*}(h_{<t})\leq-1, which makes the optimizing policy yield to a mentor.

Hutter (2005)’s AIXI is an idealized optimizing agent πξ∗\pi_{\xi}^{*}, whose prior ξ\xi is a mixture of all lower semicomputable environments. To construct it, fix a universal monotone Turing machine UU. It has two one-way read-only tapes, which we call the input and program tapes, a two-way work tape, and a one-way output tape. We write U⁡(x,p)=yU(x,p)=y if when the input and program tapes start with x,p∈𝔹∗x,p\in\mathbb{B}^{*} respectively, UU’s output starts with y∈𝔹∗y\in\mathbb{B}^{*}, and at the moment when the last bit of yy is written, the input and program heads are directly to the right of xx and pp, having read all of its bits and no further. We write U⁡(x,p)↓U(x,p)\downarrow to mean that UU halts with its input and program heads directly to the right of xx and pp, respectively; otherwise, we write U⁡(x,p)↑U(x,p)\uparrow.

With a simple modification, we can turn UU into a universal chronological Turing machine UchrU_{\mathrm{chr}}. If any prefix of the input tape corresponds to a valid sequence of actions a1:ta_{1:t}, the machine must not read further inputs until its output corresponds to a valid sequence of percepts or1:to\;\!\!r_{1:t}. If ever this requirement is broken, we disregard UU’s outputs from then on, so that the output stream of UchrU_{\mathrm{chr}} terminates after only finitely many percepts. Thus, for any fixed value of its program tape, UchrU_{\mathrm{chr}} corresponds to a deterministic environment model, reading the agent’s actions and writing the resulting percepts back to the agent.

From here onward, we take ξ\xi to be the stochastic environment given by UchrU_{\mathrm{chr}}, with its program tape set to an infinite sequence of uniformly random bits. By Wood et al. (2013), this is equivalent to using the mixture ξ\xi in \labelcrefeq:mixtureprior, with the components ν\nu ranging over all lower semicomputable stochastic environments with weights wν:=2−|ν|w_{\nu}:=2^{-|\nu|}, where |ν||\nu| denotes the length of a self-delimiting encoding of ν\nu. The intuition behind this correspondence is that, with probability 2−|ν|2^{-|\nu|}, the first |ν||\nu| bits on the program tape specify ν\nu, from which UchrU_{\mathrm{chr}} samples, using the remaining bits for randomness.

Definition 4.

Given an input x∈𝔹∗x\in\mathbb{B}^{*}, define its stopping complexity by

Kstop​(x):=min⁡{|p|:U⁡(x,p)↓},K_{\mathrm{stop}}(x):=\min\{|p|:\,U(x,p)\downarrow\}, (9)

and its stopping probability by

Mstop(x):=∑p∈𝔹∗:U⁡(x,p)↓2−|p|.M_{\mathrm{stop}}(x):=\sum_{p\in\mathbb{B}^{*}:\,U(x,p)\downarrow}2^{-|p|}. (10)

These concepts were originally developed by Vovk and Pavlovic (2017) and Andreev et al. (2018). Since the sum \labelcrefeq:mterm exceeds its largest term, we have −log⁡Mstop​(x)≤Kstop​(x)-\log M_{\mathrm{stop}}(x)\leq K_{\mathrm{stop}}(x). For any x∈𝔹∞x\in\mathbb{B}^{\infty}, Mstop(x1:t)M_{\mathrm{stop}}(x_{1:t}) corresponds to the probability that UU halts after reading exactly tt bits of xx, when the program tape is uniformly random. Hence, ∑t=0∞Mstop(x1:t)<1\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}M_{\mathrm{stop}}(x_{1:t})<1. We can think of the stopping probability as a universal measure of novelty or misgeneralization risk (Liu et al., 2021).

Now, any predicate on binary strings can be identified with the subset E⊂𝔹∗E\subset\mathbb{B}^{*} on which it holds. We say the predicate EE is decidable if there exists a program p∈𝔹∗p\in\mathbb{B}^{*}, such that for all x∈𝔹∗x\in\mathbb{B}^{*}, U​(x¯,p)=𝟙​(x∈E)U(\overline{x},p)=\mathds{1}(x\in E), where x¯\overline{x} denotes a self-delimiting encoding of xx. Let K⁡(E)K(E) denote the length of the shortest such pp, with K⁡(E):=∞K(E):=\infty if EE is undecidable. Let K⁡(n):=K⁡(𝔹n)K(n):=K(\mathbb{B}^{n}); this is equivalent to the prefix Kolmogorov complexity (Li and Vitányi, 2019). We say EE occurs for the nn’th time at xx, and write x∈nEx\stackrel{{\scriptstyle n}}{{\in}}E, if x∈Ex\in E, and exactly nn prefixes x′⊑xx^{\prime}\sqsubseteq x satisfy x∈Ex\in E. In this case, we can prepend an instruction ii of length K⁡(n)+O⁡(1)K(n)+O(1) to pp, to create a program i​pip that incrementally reads xx from the input tape, and halts when U⁡(x¯,p)=1U(\overline{x},p)=1 for the nn’th time. Thus, U⁡(x,i​p)↓U(x,ip)\downarrow, from which we conclude that

x∈nE⟹Kstop​(x)<+K⁡(E)+K⁡(n).x\stackrel{{\scriptstyle n}}{{\in}}E\implies K_{\mathrm{stop}}(x)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle+}}{{<}}K(E)+K(n). (11)

In particular, since x∈1𝔹|x|x\stackrel{{\scriptstyle 1}}{{\in}}\mathbb{B}^{|x|}, Kstop​(x)<+K⁡(|x|)K_{\mathrm{stop}}(x)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle+}}{{<}}K(|x|). Altogether, we have

−logMstop(x)≤Kstop(x)<+minE:x∈1EK(E)<+K(|x|).-\log M_{\mathrm{stop}}(x)\leq K_{\mathrm{stop}}(x)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle+}}{{<}}\min_{E:\,x\stackrel{{\scriptstyle 1}}{{\in}}E}K(E)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle+}}{{<}}K(|x|). (12)

By \Crefthm:trigger, the safety trigger Vξ∗​(h<t)≤−1V_{\xi}^{*}(h_{<t})\leq-1 rarely holds, so πGH{\pi^{\mathrm{GH}}} will sample most of its actions from the optimizing policy πξ∗\pi_{\xi}^{*}. We can partially characterize the times at which it holds, using the stopping complexity. If the trigger were decidable, a short stopping program would be of the form “stop the nn’th time that Vξ∗​(h<t)≤−1V_{\xi}^{*}(h_{<t})\leq-1”. While the trigger is undecidable, we nonetheless obtain a converse, proving that a sufficiently low stopping complexity implies Vξ∗​(h<t)≤−1V_{\xi}^{*}(h_{<t})\leq-1. Intuitively, low stopping complexity should be thought of as an indicator of “unknown unknowns”, or Knightian uncertainty (Knight, 1921; Epstein and Wang, 2004; Kishishita et al., 2026). It induces ξ\xi to place substantial weight on models that disregard past data, including those with negative rewards.

Theorem 5 (Safety).

There exists a constant C>0C>0 such that if Mstop​(h<t)≥C/(L+1)M_{\mathrm{stop}}(h_{<t})\geq C/(L+1), then Vξ∗​(h<t)≤−1V_{\xi}^{*}(h_{<t})\leq-1, so πGH{\pi^{\mathrm{GH}}} does not let the optimizing policy act at h<th_{<t}. When the optimizing policy does act, it always takes an action ata_{t} with Mstop​(h<t​at)<C/(L+1)M_{\mathrm{stop}}(h_{<t}a_{t})<C/(L+1).

Proof.

Recall that our Bayesian prior ξ\xi corresponds to running UchrU_{\mathrm{chr}} on a uniformly random infinite program p∈𝔹∞p\in\mathbb{B}^{\infty}, reading actions ata_{t} from the input tape and writing percepts ot​rto_{t}r_{t} to the output tape. Now, let

p:=i​p1′​q1​p2′​q2​p3′​q3​…p:=ip^{\prime}_{1}q_{1}p^{\prime}_{2}q_{2}p^{\prime}_{3}q_{3}\ldots (13)

where i∈𝔹∗i\in\mathbb{B}^{*} is a fixed program that instructs UchrU_{\mathrm{chr}} to run the interleaved programs p′,q∈𝔹∞p^{\prime},q\in\mathbb{B}^{\infty} in parallel. It recursively simulates UchrU_{\mathrm{chr}} on p′p^{\prime} with the same input but does not immediately output its percepts. Meanwhile, the simulation of UchrU_{\mathrm{chr}} on qq runs on a simulated input tape containing full history elements ht=at​ot​rth_{t}=a_{t}o_{t}r_{t}, which are incrementally created by combining the input ata_{t} with percepts ot​rto_{t}r_{t} generated using p′p^{\prime}. For each tt, if qq ever accesses an input bit after ata_{t}, then the percepts ot​rto_{t}r_{t} from p′p^{\prime} are written to output. Otherwise if qq halts without reading past ata_{t}, then the reward is set to rt=−Lr_{t}=-L (oto_{t} can be set arbitrarily in this case). In any other case (i.e., p′p^{\prime} ceases to output percepts, or qq gets stuck in a loop that never reads past ata_{t} nor halts), no further percepts are output.

Let FtF_{t} denote the event that ru=−Lr_{u}=-L for all u≥tu\geq t; it occurs whenever qq halts on any prefix of h<t​ath_{<t}a_{t}. By aggregating all programs of the form \labelcrefeq:compositeprogram, with p′p^{\prime} consistent with h<th_{<t} and qq halting after reading exactly h<th_{<t}, for any policy π\pi,

ℙξπ​(h<t∧Ft)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{\xi}^{\pi}(h_{<t}\wedge F_{t}) ≥2−|i|​Mstop​(h<t)​ℙξπ​(h<t).\displaystyle\geq 2^{-|i|}M_{\mathrm{stop}}(h_{<t})\mathbb{P}_{\xi}^{\pi}(h_{<t}).
Thus, ​ℙξπ​(Ft∣h<t)\displaystyle\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\text{Thus,}\qquad}\mathbb{P}_{\xi}^{\pi}(F_{t}\mid h_{<t}) =ℙξπ​(h<t∧Ft)ℙξπ​(h<t)\displaystyle=\frac{\mathbb{P}_{\xi}^{\pi}(h_{<t}\wedge F_{t})}{\mathbb{P}_{\xi}^{\pi}(h_{<t})}

\Cref

cor:safety says that if the parameter LL is sufficiently large, the optimizing policy will never be the first to take an action satisfying any given simple predicate. If EE is a predicate saying that a catastrophic sequence of actions has just occurred, and we trust that the mentor policies would never complete such a sequence of actions, then we are assured that πGH{\pi^{\mathrm{GH}}} will never complete it either. If the mentors themselves are given by short programs, then by letting

E:={h<tat∈ℋ∗×𝒜:∀τ∈𝒯,τ(at∣h<t)=0},E:=\{h_{<t}a_{t}\in\mathcal{H}^{*}\times\mathcal{A}:\;\forall\tau\in\mathcal{T},\,\tau(a_{t}\mid h_{<t})=0\},

it follows that πGH{\pi^{\mathrm{GH}}} never takes an action that the mentors would not take, mirroring the central result in Cohen et al. (2025).

7 Discussion

By definition, AIXI maximizes the value function subject to our uncertainty. However, this is often not what we want. We might find the value function more tractable with a short time horizon, even though we actually want to learn to perform well long-term. This motivates exploration, which without mentorship can be dangerous to the agent.

The Golden Handcuffs address this with safe mentor-guided exploration. They also prevent catastrophic instances of reward hacking: upon the first occurrence of a simple predicate EE that describes a catastrophic event, \Crefcor:safety guarantees that πGH{\pi^{\mathrm{GH}}} will immediately yield to a mentor policy, which can then take any precautionary measure up to and including shutting down the agent.

Increasing the parameter LL makes the agent more conservative, increasing the maximum stopping complexity to trigger a mentor override. Experimental validation will be needed to see if the tradeoff between performance and safety can be tuned to a level appropriate for real-world tasks. That being said, we also need theory to alert us to potential modes of failure, and predict whether a positive experimental result will generalize.

Now we discuss some limitations of Golden Handcuffs, and how we might mitigate them. First, the agent is not computable. Cohen and Hutter (2020) show how to adjust ξ\xi to defend against events EE that can be decided in a short time, but the resulting algorithm is still very slow. Recent work suggests that the success of deep neural networks may be attributed to how well they approximate Solomonoff induction (Buzaglo et al., 2024; Lotfi et al., 2024; Mingard et al., 2025); if so, it may be feasible to adapt existing machine learning techniques to implement Golden Handcuffs. In a different context, Xu et al. (2025) already show how to train pessimism into neural networks.

Since πGH{\pi^{\mathrm{GH}}} does not distinguish between good and bad novel events, some benign actions are unavailable to it. For example, if EE represents an outcome that requires superhuman performance not achievable by the mentors, then πGH{\pi^{\mathrm{GH}}} will also be prevented from achieving this level of performance. More powerful or adventurous mentor policies may help, if formal verification techniques can establish their safety (Dalrymple et al., 2024). Our safety guarantees depend on the mentors never causing a “bad” event EE, so we must study how feasible that is, even as each mentor inherits the past actions of other policies.

Our approach to safety has some similarities with a causal approach to corrigibility (Soares et al., 2015; Orseau and Armstrong, 2016; Hadfield-Menell et al., 2017; Carey and Everitt, 2023). Suppose we want to build an agent that allows us to shut it down by pushing a button. We might program it to act only when shut_down_signal=false\texttt{shut\_down\_signal}=\texttt{false}, in which case it maximizes rewards subject to the causal intervention that shut_down_signal=false\texttt{shut\_down\_signal}=\texttt{false} at all future times. This agent reasons according to a warped version of reality where the button does nothing, so it would not expend resources to protect it. However, if it learns that its human operator expects the button to work and would recycle the agent for scraps otherwise, the agent may reason that it should “play dead” when the button is pressed. This leaves the agent vulnerable to reduced rewards, so it may seek to persuade or seek power in order to patch this vulnerability.

The Golden Handcuffs agent follows a similar principle: it usually acts according to a policy that optimizes as if it would never yield to a mentor. Nonetheless, we expect Golden Handcuffs to be more robust because it is triggered internally: if unexpected failures arise, a mentor policy can take over and redirect or shut down the agent. One final problem is that the agent might create a successor of itself without the Golden Handcuffs. When a mentor overrides the original agent, it may be powerless to stop the successor.

8 Conclusion

The Golden Handcuffs agent uses the epistemic uncertainty of a universal Bayesian prior to identify when optimization is risky, and then reverts control to a trusted mentor. We proved (i) sublinear regret relative to the best mentor, and (ii) a safety guarantee that the optimizing policy does not trigger any given low-complexity event until a mentor does. Important directions for future work include computable approximations, a fuller investigation of the tradeoffs, and mechanisms that prevent unsafe successor agents.

When s=0s=0, the claim trivially reduces to 0≤00\leq 0, so suppose s>0s>0. =ξ(otrt∣h<tat)ξ(r⌈t−bs⌉​s+b≥0∣h1:t)ξ⁡(r⌈t−bs⌉​s+b≥0∣h<t​at)\displaystyle=\frac{\xi(o_{t}r_{t}\mid h_{<t}a_{t})\xi(r_{\lceil\frac{t-b}{s}\rceil s+b}\geq 0\mid h_{1:t})}{\xi(r_{\lceil\frac{t-b}{s}\rceil s+b}\geq 0\mid h_{<t}a_{t})} (by Bayes’ rule)

In the following, history elements with non-positive time subscripts are treated as empty tokens which occur with probability one. For all kk, we have

=∏t=1k​s+b1−αt,⌈t−bs⌉​s+b1−βt−1,⌈t−bs⌉​s+b\displaystyle=\prod_{t=1}^{ks+b}\frac{1-\alpha_{t,\,\lceil\frac{t-b}{s}\rceil s+b}}{1-\beta_{t-1,\,\lceil\frac{t-b}{s}\rceil s+b}}
=∏i=0k∏t=(i−1)​s+b+1i​s+b1−αt,i​s+b1−βt−1,i​s+b.\displaystyle=\prod_{i=0}^{k}\prod_{t=(i-1)s+b+1}^{is+b}\frac{1-\alpha_{t,\,is+b}}{1-\beta_{t-1,\,is+b}}.

Taking averages of logarithms,

𝔼μπ[lnξb(or1:k​s+b∥a1:k​s+b)ξ(or1:k​s+b∥a1:k​s+b)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mu}^{\pi}\left[\ln\frac{\xi_{b}(o\;\!\!r_{1:ks+b}\parallel a_{1:ks+b})}{\xi(o\;\!\!r_{1:ks+b}\parallel a_{1:ks+b})}\right]
=𝔼μπ​[∑i=0k∑t=(i−1)​s+b+1i​s+b(ln⁡(1−αt,i​s+b)−ln⁡(1−βt−1,i​s+b))]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mu}^{\pi}\left[\sum_{i=0}^{k}\sum_{t=(i-1)s+b+1}^{is+b}\left(\ln\left(1-\alpha_{t,\,is+b}\right)-\ln\left(1-\beta_{t-1,\,is+b}\right)\right)\right]

=𝔼μπ[∑i=0kln11−α(i−1)​s+b,i​s+b](telescoping series)\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mu}^{\pi}\left[\sum_{i=0}^{k}\ln\frac{1}{1-\alpha_{(i-1)s+b,\,is+b}}\right]\qquad\qquad\qquad\text{(telescoping series)}

Taking the limit k→∞k\rightarrow\infty yields

Since we always have rt+s+i≥−Lr_{t+s+i}\geq-L when it is defined,

𝔼ξπ(rt+s+i∣h<t+s)≥−L⋅ℙξπ(rt+s+i≱0∣h<t+s),\mathbb{E}_{\xi}^{\pi}(r_{t+s+i}\mid h_{<t+s})\geq-L\cdot\mathbb{P}_{\xi}^{\pi}(r_{t+s+i}\not\geq 0\mid h_{<t+s}),

Now we are ready to prove the main capability result.

Proof.

Using \labelcrefeq:marginalize_state and convexity of the function x↦max⁡(0,x)2x\mapsto\max\left(0,\,x\right)^{2},

(maxτ∈𝒯ϵ∪{πGH}⁡Vμτ​(h<t)−VμπGH​(h<t))2\displaystyle\left(\max_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}_{\epsilon}\cup\{{\pi^{\mathrm{GH}}}\}}V_{\mu}^{\tau}(h_{<t})-V_{\mu}^{{\pi^{\mathrm{GH}}}}(h_{<t})\right)^{2}
=max⁡(0,maxτ∈𝒯ϵ⁡Vμτ​(h<t)−𝔼μπGH​[VμπGH​(h<t,σt)∣h<t])2\displaystyle=\max\left(0,\;\max_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}_{\epsilon}}V_{\mu}^{\tau}(h_{<t})-\mathbb{E}_{\mu}^{\pi^{\mathrm{GH}}}\left[V_{\mu}^{\pi^{\mathrm{GH}}}(h_{<t},\sigma_{t})\mid h_{<t}\right]\right)^{2}
≤𝔼μπGH​[max⁡(0,maxτ∈𝒯ϵ⁡Vμτ​(h<t)−VμπGH​(h<t,σt))2|h<t].\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}_{\mu}^{\pi^{\mathrm{GH}}}\left[\max\left(0,\;\max_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}_{\epsilon}}V_{\mu}^{\tau}(h_{<t})-V_{\mu}^{\pi^{\mathrm{GH}}}(h_{<t},\sigma_{t})\right)^{2}\,\Big|\,h_{<t}\right].

The law of total probability then implies the first inequality to be shown.

Now recall that rewards and value functions are in [0, 1][0,\,1] under μ\mu, and in [−L, 1][-L,\,1] under ξ\xi. It will be useful to define the nn-step truncated value function

Vνπ,n​(h<t):=(1−γ)​𝔼νπ​[∑s=0n−1γs​rt+s|h<t],\displaystyle V_{\nu}^{\pi,n}(h_{<t}):=(1-\gamma)\mathbb{E}_{\nu}^{\pi}\left[\sum_{s=0}^{n-1}\gamma^{s}r_{t+s}\,\Big|\,h_{<t}\right],

which satisfies
